title: Strands, skins and legs: constraints that are exact against penalties that stretch
summary: Math Studio's Deform & Hair and Mechanisms workspaces animate three classical geometry-processing ideas. Follow-the-leader hair keeps segment lengths exactly while a spring model lets them stretch; linear blend skinning collapses a twisted joint where dual quaternion skinning keeps its volume; and a Stewart-Gough platform shows how six legs give six degrees of freedom.

media.alt: Two-panel figure. Left, panel a titled snapshots every 0.25 seconds (FTL): blue curves from the origin fan out and down as a strand falls, plus one orange curve for a spring strand falling straight further down. Right, panel b titled inextensibility: largest segment-length error against time on a log axis from 1e-17 to 1e-1; a flat blue FTL line near 1e-16, and orange and yellow spring curves near 1e-2 to 1e-1.

read_the_figure.question: Which model keeps the strand the length it is supposed to be, and what do you pay for the models that do not?
read_the_figure.axes: Panel a: x and z position in the plane of the strand, each curve a snapshot. Panel b: time 0 to 2 seconds against largest segment-length error on a log axis. The other figures have 3D scenes with a short caption of where the technique is used.
look_at: Panel b: FTL (blue) sits at about 1e-16 for all times, i.e. exactly constant length to round-off. Springs with stiffness 300 (orange) and 1500 (yellow) sit at 1e-2 to 1e-1, five to thirteen orders of magnitude worse; stiffer springs are better but not exact.
The legend prints the maxima: FTL 6.9e-17, springs k = 300: 8.1e-2, k = 1500: 2.3e-2. Raising k by a factor 5 lowered the error by a factor 3.5.
Panel a: the strand starts horizontal along the x axis and swings down; the light blue snapshots show the shape every 0.25 s; one spring snapshot at 2 s hangs lower than FTL because it has stretched.
Deform & Hair screenshots: a head of strands, guide strands (60), children (360) and 35 particles per strand; the panel prints a maximum segment-length error of 1.39e-16 for FTL.

Skinning screenshot: two cylinders bent at a joint; the left (linear blend skinning) pinches at the elbow, the right (dual quaternion) keeps its thickness; the plot on the left of that screenshot shows the blend curves.
Mechanism screenshot: a platform on six legs with a mobility tape; the caption says six legs give six degrees of freedom.
read_the_figure.proves: Exact constraints (FTL) keep lengths to round-off by construction; penalty models (springs) trade length error against stiffness and time step. Skinning shows that averaging matrices is not the same as averaging rotations. The platform shows how constraints reduce a 6-DOF body's freedom to those the legs allow.
if_wrong: A length error that grows with time: a spring model that is not stiff enough or integrated with too large a step.
A pinched joint in a skinned model: linear blending of rotation matrices.
A mobility count that disagrees with the visible motion: a mistaken joint list.
Reading orders of magnitude from a log axis as small differences.
must_check: That the error axis is logarithmic and the maxima are printed.
That the time step and stiffness of the spring model are stated.
That the skinning comparison shows the same pose for both methods.
That a mechanism's joints and links are listed for the mobility count.

terms.meaning: Each particle is moved to the point at the fixed segment length from its predecessor along the direction of its predicted position.
A force proportional to the stretch of a segment; allows stretch.
Each vertex is moved by a weighted average of bone transformations.
Blending of rigid motions as dual quaternions, which keeps the result a rigid motion.
The number of degrees of freedom of a mechanism from its bodies and joints.

remember: FTL fixes each segment length to round-off by construction.
A spring stretches by roughly the force over k; stiffer springs need smaller time steps.
The average of two rotation matrices is not a rotation; its determinant is below 1.
Dual quaternions blend rigid motions without shrinking.
Mobility counts bodies, joints and the freedom of each joint.

steps.title: FTL update
steps.note: The corrected particle lies on a sphere of radius ell around the previous one: the segment length is ell up to round-off, which is why the blue line sits at 1e-16.

steps.title: Static stretch of a spring segment
steps.note: The ideal ratio of 5 compares with the observed 3.5 (8.1e-2 against 2.3e-2): the error also depends on dynamics, but the trend with k is clear.

steps.title: Why blending matrices pinches
steps.note: Averaging the identity and a rotation by theta gives a matrix that scales by cos(theta/2): at 90 degrees the scale is 0.71, at 180 degrees the volume collapses to a flat sheet (the candy-wrapper effect).

steps.title: Mobility of a 6-UPS platform
steps.note: N = 14 bodies (base, platform, 6 times two leg parts), J = 18 joints, each leg with a universal (2), prismatic (1) and spherical (3) joint. The caption of the screenshot says six legs give six degrees of freedom.

worked.title: Skinning scale at a 90 degree bend
worked.problem: Averaging the identity and a rotation by 90 degrees with weights one half each, find the length scale factor of the blended matrix.

solution.text: A rotation by 45 degrees times the scale cos 45.

worked.answer: 0.71: a vertex at weight one half is pulled to 71 percent of its distance from the joint axis; cylinders pinch at bends.

checks.answer: That each segment keeps its length to round-off.

checks.q: Spring stretch 0.081 at k = 300. Expected stretch at k = 1500 for the same load?
Why is a log axis used in panel b?
checks.answer: The errors span sixteen decades, from round-off to a few percent.

checks.q: Both hair models look similar in a still frame. How would you decide which to use?
checks.answer: By the length error and cost: FTL is exact in length, springs allow stretch but give simple dynamics; the figure's panel b gives the length side.

checks.answer: Twist a cylinder progressively to 180 degrees and plot its cross-section area for both skinning methods against angle.
